mechanism: One real or cherry-picked trade is copied to several accounts, so every testimonial shows the same instrument, entry time and price. The only thing that differs is position size, so the dollar profit looks very different while the underlying move (here 77 cents on gold) is identical. A balance screenshot from a day tab is then shown as if it were accumulated wealth. The tell is the shared timestamp and price across supposedly independent members.
claim: Members of a Telegram copy-trading channel post large profits and a 100 percent win rate from the bot's signals.
why_not_testable: The funnel lives behind a Telegram channel and a broker link, and checking it needs a connected account, which is off limits.
needs: A Telegram session and a broker or Myfxbook link, neither of which should be touched.
one_line: A copy-trade funnel sold three testimonials that were one gold trade at one timestamp, with lot size the only difference.
idea_why: Selling one trade as many independent wins is a presentation trick, not an edge; the only real check is a verified track record with a public link.
breakdown: The sensible use of this is a detection checklist, not a build. Line up each testimonial's instrument, timestamp and price; if they match, divide profit by lot size to confirm the same price move. Ask for a verified Myfxbook or broker statement link and check it was not made read-only on a demo account. Compare subscriber count to engagement for a sanity read on audience quality. No hired role is needed; a person checking screenshots is enough.

mechanism: A zero-dependency Node kernel takes events (cron, GitHub issues, errors) and routes them by a rules.json file to a command-line agent in a given directory. The agent runs one round and exits; if it needs a decision it ends its last reply with a fenced agent-autoloop JSON block (ask, notice, resolve, later, events). The kernel parses that block, pushes a card to chat or desktop, holds no process or tokens while waiting, then resumes the same agent session with the answer. Malformed blocks get one rewrite request in the same session rather than a redo.
claim: Command-line agents pick up work in the background and only ask a human when unsure, with no server or public port; 3,168 stars in two days.
why_not_testable: It needs Node 24, a curl-to-shell installer and a logged-in agent CLI, and a real run spends model tokens.
needs: Node 24 and a logged-in agent CLI (spends tokens).
one_line: Agent Autoloop lets a CLI agent end each round with a JSON block that asks a human or schedules a later wake-up, holding nothing open while it waits.
idea_why: Exit-after-each-round with a structured hand-back block is a clean way to run unattended agents without idle processes.
breakdown: Read the kernel source for the block parser and the resume path first, since that is the novel part. Then run its dry-run commands (rules explain, emit --dry-run) on a throwaway rules file, which touch no agent. A real round-trip would wire one rule to a local agent with a trivial prompt and answer the card from the terminal. Proteus already has scheduled runs and a hook; the comparison to draw is how this resumes sessions and merges queued events.

mechanism: Character consistency in generated video comes from fixing a reference set (a character sheet of stills, a look block of fixed descriptors, a cloned voice) and feeding the same references into every shot prompt. Cloning adds a voice model and a lip-sync or avatar step on top of the stills. AI ad variants are then produced by swapping hook and script while the character and voice stay fixed, so an ad set is a table of hooks against one actor. Drift between shots is checked by eye from a contact sheet.

one_line: Consistent AI characters come from a fixed reference sheet and look block reused in every prompt, with ad variants made by swapping hooks.
idea_why: Reusing one reference set across shots is the standard working method for consistent generated characters.

mechanism: Each tool call is mapped into a shared semantic form, and an executable ontology plus per-episode task state yields one of three deterministic verdicts: ready, waiting or forbidden. Waiting means an unmet but recoverable precondition, so the agent can replan without widening its permissions. The ontology is grown offline: an LLM proposes action and state axioms from failed training runs, and each is accepted only if it fixes a logged error, stays logically consistent and passes held-out validation before the ontology is frozen.
claim: 0 percent attack success rate on AgentDojo, ASB and AgentDyn while improving task utility under attack.
why_not_testable: No code is linked in the abstract and the benchmarks need model answers, which are not keyless tonight.
needs: The paper's code (not confirmed to exist) and a model to run benchmarks.
one_line: SecureGARD gates agent tool calls with a rule ontology that returns ready, waiting or forbidden, and claims zero successful prompt injections on three benchmarks.
idea_why: A three-state gate that separates not-yet from never is a useful design, but zero attacks on public benchmarks needs independent confirmation.
breakdown: Fetch the paper and check for a repository. If code exists, run its gate on the public AgentDojo task set with a stub agent that replays recorded tool calls, which avoids needing a live model. For Proteus, the transferable piece is the waiting verdict: the existing hook only allows or denies, so a denial with a named unmet precondition would let a run route around it instead of retrying. That would be a small change to the hook's reason text, not an ontology.

mechanism: Take the open MOT test results, and for each make and model compare its fail rate with an expected rate for cars of the same age band, mileage band and fuel type. The headline gaps are the ratio of observed to expected failures, so a Corsa reads about 22 percent below the average-car pass rate and a 3 Series 23 percent above, with the cohort adjustment stopping old cars from dominating. Fault-category rates (steering, brakes) use the same cohort comparison.
claim: A Vauxhall Corsa fails its MOT almost 60 percent more often than a BMW 3 Series, across about 30 million tests and 8 million fails last year.
verdict_question: Using one public year of DVSA MOT results with age, mileage and fuel cohorts, does the Corsa fail rate come out roughly 60 percent above the 3 Series?
probe_title: MOT cohort fail rates: does a Corsa fail about 60 percent more than a 3 Series once age, mileage and fuel are matched?
one_line: A UK MOT video claims a Corsa fails 60 percent more than a 3 Series once age, mileage and fuel are matched; the open data can check it.
idea_why: Comparing each model with a matched age, mileage and fuel cohort is the correct way to avoid blaming old cars on their model.
breakdown: Download the anonymised MOT results from data.gov.uk (the keyless bulk files, not the keyed API) and load one year with pandas or DuckDB. Bucket test mileage and vehicle age, group by fuel, compute the cohort fail rate, then for each model divide observed fails by the sum of cohort rates. Compare Corsa and 3 Series ratios to the video's figures and check the Bentley Continental at about a third of the usual rate. If the file is too large for the time box, restrict to a single month and say so. No hired role needed.

mechanism: A deliberately cheap product (5 dollars, cut from 12.50) is a qualifier: paying puts a card on file and marks the buyer as willing to spend, then routes them to a private one-to-one call where the real, expensive offer is made. The cheap kit is the commodity (pay-per-view clipping); the high-ticket offer sits behind the call. Income claims are anecdotes and the guarantee covers something other than earnings. Platforms and card networks see this as a low-ticket lead-gen funnel.
claim: A 5 dollar clipping-agency starter kit leads to income of 3k in the first week for beginners.
why_not_testable: Seeing the funnel means paying and booking a call, which needs a card and an account.
needs: A card payment and a booked sales call.
one_line: A 5 dollar kit works as a card-on-file qualifier that routes buyers to a one-to-one sales call, where the real offer lands.
idea_why: A low-ticket qualifier feeding a high-ticket call is an ordinary, legal funnel shape; the question is only whether the claims on it are honest.
breakdown: As a pattern for legitimate use: a cheap, useful sample filters for buyers, and a call converts the few who want more. To study it without joining, read the public landing page, the refund and guarantee wording, and the pricing history. A hired closer or sales person handles the call itself, which no script covers. Honest claims, evidenced results and a guarantee that matches the headline are what separate this from the scheme version.
